newsitem.title: SPAIN: Analysts count gains from BCH sale of Azucarera.
newsitem.headline: Analysts count gains from BCH sale of Azucarera.

text.p: Banco Central Hispano's upcoming sale of its 49.9 percent stake in sugar refiner Azucarera will be positive both for the banking group and Spain's sugar industry as whole, analysts said on Tuesday.

BCH announced on Monday it was studying purchase offers from Mercasa, Caja de Salamanca and sugar refiner Ebro at 5,100 pesetas per share, valuing the sale at a total of 21 billion pesetas ($165 million) for a capital gain of two billion pesetas.
"It's a very good operation," said Alejandro Ruira, banking analyst at AB Asesores. "Holding 49.9 percent didn't make much sense for them."
The splitting of its stake into three means BCH can avoid Spanish regulations which say a public offering must be made for the sale of stakes of more than 25 percent.
Caja Salamanca will buy 24.9 percent, Ebro 21 percent and Mercasa four percent, Spanish financial daily Expansion said on Tuesday. BCH was not immediately able to confirm this.

The bank is expected to invest the profits of the sale in increasing its stake in electricity group Endesa to three percent from 1.5 percent and will also channel funds into Retevision, Spain's planned second telephony operator.

"It wants to maintain the volume of shares it holds (in industry) but bit by bit, transfer to less mature sectors with higher potential for growth," said Ruira. "In the long term, this will be better than holding the Azucarera stake."
Although potential revenue from doubling the Endesa stake is similar to that from Azucalera, it could earn more from banking activities for the electricity group.
"One musn't forget that afterwards, there is a very important level of follow-through business," said Jose Luis Fisure, banking analyst at BBV Interactivos.
"There will be a certain quid pro quo between the two to support each other," he said. "This is very difficult to put a value on."

The deal, which follows several years of see-sawing during which France's Generale Sucriere increased its stake in Azucarera in a bid to take control, could also benefit the domestic sugar industry as a whole.
The Ministry of Agriculture has strongly campaigned to keep the company in Spanish hands.
"For Spain's general interests, this is better than having sold it to Generale Sucriere," said Fisure. "This could have led in the future to the disappearance of Azucarera."

Azucarera's share value has risen 13 percent since late August in anticipation of the sale and should remain near those levels until the year-end, even though it may endure a bout of speculative selling once the deal actually goes through, an analyst said.
"It's already more than discounted," she said. Azucarera traded down 85 pesetas at 4,810 at 1015 GMT.
Meanwhile, the Azucarera sale will help BCH continue to gain ground from around 2,700 at present as profits pick up and costs come under control following a turbulent period of restructuring.

"BCH has already emerged from the tunnel and is stepping on the path towards reasonable growth," said Fisure. "There will be some capital gains in the second half (in addition to the two million pesetas from Azucarera)."

He saw the share price rising to 3,000 pesetas by the end of the year, based on BBV's predictions of a net profit of 34.8 billion pesetas in 1996, up 180 percent from 1995, rising to between 43 and 44 billion pesetas in 1997.
